## Proof

**Claim:** Yes. If $c \in M$, then $J_c \subseteq D$.

**Key facts.** For $f_c(z)=z^2+c$, the filled Julia set is
$$K_c = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : \{f_c^{\,n}(z)\}_{n\ge 0} \text{ is bounded}\},$$
and $J_c = \partial K_c$. The set $K_c$ is closed (it is the intersection $\bigcap_{n} (f_c^{\,n})^{-1}(\overline{B(0,R)})$ for any escape radius $R>2$ with $R\ge |c|$, hence closed), so $\partial K_c \subseteq K_c$, giving $J_c \subseteq K_c$.

**Escape-radius lemma.** If $|c|\le 2$ and $|z|>2$, then the orbit of $z$ under $f_c$ escapes to infinity, so $z\notin K_c$.

*Proof of lemma.* Since $|c|\le 2 < |z|$, we have $|z|>|c|$. Then
$$|f_c(z)| = |z^2+c| \ge |z|^2 - |c| > |z|^2 - |z| = |z|(|z|-1).$$
Because $|z|>2$, we have $|z|-1>1$, hence $|f_c(z)| > |z| > 2$. In particular $|f_c(z)| > |z| > |c|$, so the same hypotheses hold at $f_c(z)$. Iterating, the moduli $|f_c^{\,n}(z)|$ form a strictly increasing sequence with $|f_c^{\,n+1}(z)| \ge |f_c^{\,n}(z)|\bigl(|f_c^{\,n}(z)|-1\bigr)$. Once a term exceeds $2$, the multiplicative factor $|w|-1$ exceeds $1$ and grows, forcing $|f_c^{\,n}(z)|\to\infty$. Thus the orbit escapes. $\square$

**Conclusion.** By hypothesis $M\subseteq D$, so $c\in M$ implies $|c|\le 2$. By the lemma, every point with $|z|>2$ lies outside $K_c$, hence
$$K_c \subseteq \{z : |z|\le 2\} = D.$$
Since $K_c$ is closed, $J_c = \partial K_c \subseteq K_c \subseteq D$.

Therefore $c\in M \implies J_c \subseteq D$. $\blacksquare$
